questions.question_text: A committee of $4$ is to be chosen from a group of $10$ people. If one specific person, Mark, must be included, how many different committees can be formed?

options.why: Calculated 10C4, ignoring the restriction that Mark must be included.
Calculated 9C4, excluding Mark instead of including him.
Multiplied 8 by 3 instead of evaluating the combination 9C3.

questions.solution_text:
Fix Mark on the committee and choose $3$ from $9$ remaining:
$= {^{9}C_{3}}$
$= \dfrac{9 \times 8 \times 7}{3 \times 2 \times 1}$
$= 84$

questions.question_text: From a club of $12$ members, a committee of $5$ is selected. Two members, David and Sarah, cannot serve together. How many committees are possible?

options.why: Calculated total combinations 12C5 without subtracting cases where both serve.
Calculated only the number of committees where both David and Sarah serve.
Calculated 10C5, excluding both individuals entirely.

questions.solution_text:
Total committees $= {^{12}C_{5}} = 792$.
Committees containing both David and Sarah $= {^{10}C_{3}} = 120$.
Committees where both do not serve $= 792 - 120$
$= 672$

questions.question_text: A panel of $4$ judges is selected from $5$ lawyers and $4$ academics. In how many ways can the panel be formed if it must contain at least $3$ lawyers?

options.why: Subtracted 10 from 45 due to an arithmetic error.
Calculated 9C4 without enforcing the minimum requirement of 3 lawyers.
Multiplied 10 by 5 instead of adding the two mutually exclusive cases.

questions.solution_text:
Case 1 ($3$ lawyers, $1$ academic): $^{5}C_{3} \times {^{4}C_{1}} = 10 \times 4 = 40$
Case 2 ($4$ lawyers, $0$ academics): $^{5}C_{4} \times {^{4}C_{0}} = 5 \times 1 = 5$
Total $= 40 + 5$
$= 45$

questions.question_text: A delegation of $3$ is chosen from $5$ men and $3$ women. How many delegations contain more men than women?

options.why: Calculated only the case with 2 men and 1 woman, omitting the case with 3 men.
Calculated 8C3 without considering the gender restriction.
Calculated only the case with 3 men, omitting the case with 2 men.

questions.solution_text:
More men than women in $3$ members requires $2$ men or $3$ men.
Case 1 ($2$ men, $1$ woman): $^{5}C_{2} \times {^{3}C_{1}} = 10 \times 3 = 30$
Case 2 ($3$ men, $0$ women): $^{5}C_{3} \times {^{3}C_{0}} = 10 \times 1 = 10$
Total $= 30 + 10$
$= 40$

questions.question_text: A committee of $3$ is selected from $7$ doctors and $4$ nurses. How many different committees contain at least one nurse?

options.why: Calculated total combinations 11C3 without subtracting the all-doctor cases.
Calculated the number of committees with no nurses instead of at least one.
Calculated 4C1 times 7C2, double counting committees with multiple nurses.

questions.solution_text:
Total committees: $^{11}C_{3} = 165$.
All doctors (no nurses): $^{7}C_{3} = 35$.
At least one nurse $= 165 - 35$
$= 130$

questions.question_text: $3$ letters are chosen at random without replacement from the $8$ letters in $\text{TRIANGLE}$. In how many ways can the selection contain at least one vowel?

options.why: Calculated total combinations 8C3 without subtracting all-consonant selections.
Counted only selections with zero vowels instead of subtracting from total.
Multiplied 3C1 by 5C2, failing to account for selections with multiple vowels.

questions.solution_text:
Vowels: I, A, E ($3$); Consonants: T, R, N, G, L ($5$).
Total selections: $^{8}C_{3} = 56$.
All consonants: $^{5}C_{3} = 10$.
At least one vowel $= 56 - 10$
$= 46$

questions.question_text: In how many ways can $6$ students be divided into two groups of $2$ and $4$ students respectively?

options.why: Multiplied 6C2 by 2, incorrectly permuting the group assignments.
Calculated 6C3 / 2!, dividing as if the groups had equal size.
Divided 6C2 by 2, incorrectly halving an unequal partition.

questions.solution_text:
Because the group sizes are unequal ($2$ and $4$), no division by factorials is required:
$= {^{6}C_{2}} \times {^{4}C_{4}}$
$= 15 \times 1$
$= 15$

questions.question_text: In how many ways can $10$ players be divided into two teams of $5$ players each, if the two teams are unlabeled?

options.why: Calculated 10C5 without dividing by 2! for the indistinguishable teams.
Multiplied 10 by 5 instead of evaluating the combination partition.
Divided by 4 instead of 2!.

questions.solution_text:
Choose $5$ players for one team in $^{10}C_{5} = 252$ ways.
Since the two teams of $5$ are indistinguishable, divide by $2!$:
$= \dfrac{252}{2}$
$= 126$

options.why: Calculated total triples 9C3 without subtracting the collinear points.
Subtracted 4C2 instead of 4C3 from total combinations.
Halved the total triangles due to confusion over vertex ordering.

questions.solution_text:
Total triples: $^{9}C_{3} = 84$.
Collinear triples: $^{4}C_{3} = 4$.
Number of triangles $= 84 - 4$
$= 80$

questions.question_text: A committee of $5$ is selected from $7$ teachers and $6$ students. The committee must include at least $2$ teachers and at least $2$ students. If two specific teachers, Mr Brown and Ms Green, refuse to serve together, how many different committees can be formed?

options.why: Calculated the number of committees with at least 2 teachers and at least 2 students without subtracting the cases where both Mr Brown and Ms Green serve together.
Subtracted all 11C3 = 165 committees containing both teachers, including those with invalid category distributions.
Calculated only the case with 3 teachers and 2 students, omitting the case with 2 teachers and 3 students.

questions.solution_text:
Committees with at least $2$ teachers and at least $2$ students:
Case 1 ($2$ teachers, $3$ students): $^{7}C_{2} \times {^{6}C_{3}} = 21 \times 20 = 420$
Case 2 ($3$ teachers, $2$ students): $^{7}C_{3} \times {^{6}C_{2}} = 35 \times 15 = 525$
Total without conflict restriction $= 420 + 525 = 945$
Committees containing both Mr Brown and Ms Green:
Case 1 ($2$ teachers total, $3$ students): $^{5}C_{0} \times {^{6}C_{3}} = 1 \times 20 = 20$
Case 2 ($3$ teachers total, $2$ students): $^{5}C_{1} \times {^{6}C_{2}} = 5 \times 15 = 75$
Subtotal containing both $= 20 + 75 = 95$
Valid committees $= 945 - 95$
$= 850$
